messages.author: 56dd228b31f47f06
messages.subject: Help understanding measEq.syntax strict invariance
parts:
Hello! We're testing a repeated-measures (longitudinal) measurement invariance with a simple model:

Model.PrPo.Wide <- '
At1 =~ PrCon + PrEnj + PrImp + PrMot + PrIde
Att2 =~ PoCon + PoEnj + PoImp + PoMot + PoIde
'
LongFacNames <- list(Attitude = c("Att1", "Att2"))

However, I'm not sure conceptually what's going on that there is no difference between my strong model and strict model. Syntax for both shown below. 

PrPoScaInv <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = Model.PrPo.Wide, 
                            data = Wide, 
                            parameterization = "theta", 
                            ID.fac ="std.lv", 
                            ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016", 
                            longFacNames = LongFacNames, 
                            return.fit = TRUE, 
                            estimator = "MLM", 
                            long.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"))

PrPoStrInv <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = Model.PrPo.Wide, 
                            data = Wide, 
                            parameterization = "theta", 
                            ID.fac ="std.lv", 
                            ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016", 
                            longFacNames = LongFacNames, 
                            return.fit = TRUE, 
                            estimator = "MLM", 
                            long.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts", "lv.autocov"))

My guess is it is because it's a single factor model across two time points... but conceptually I don't get why I can't constrain the factor variances (in this case auto covariances, which I guess I also don't quite understand). Adding "resid.autocov" also doesn't change the model from the strong model, either. 

Thanks in advance,
Dana

messages.author: 12fdd832cacb825e
messages.subject: Re: Help understanding measEq.syntax strict invariance
parts:
Constraining factor variances is not part of invariance testing. The variances may, in fact, differ naturally and correctly between the two times if responses are converging or diverging over time.

That said, std.lv=TRUE is also not appropriate for invariance testing precisely because of the above. It forces actual differences in the factor variances to manifest in the loadings or (if loadings are constrained) residuals.

Since you used std.lv=TRUE, constraining the latent variances doesn't affect fit since the variances are both forced to 1 and therefore already equal.

Pat

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Help understanding measEq.syntax strict invariance
parts: There's a lot going on here, so I'm responding to multiple messages in this thread at once:
I'm not sure conceptually what's going on that there is no difference between my strong model and strict model.

"lv.autocov" does not constrain variances, it constrains covariances (see the help-page description, under the Repeated Measures section of Details).  Because you only have 2 occasions, there is only a single autocovariance/autocorrelation (i.e., covariance between the same construct at different occasions); thus, no parameters can be constrained to equality, so you still only have a scalar-invariance model. 

                            parameterization = "theta", 
                            ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016", 

These arguments are only relevant if you have categorical indicators.  You do not declare any as ordered=, and you are using an estimator for continuous indicators:

                            estimator = "MLM",
I don't get why I can't constrain the factor variances
As in described in ?lavOptions, factor variances can be constrained with the keyword "lv.variances"
Adding "resid.autocov" also doesn't change the model from the strong model, either.

Because you only have 2 occasions (same note as above).

Patrick:  std.lv=TRUE is also not appropriate for invariance testing precisely because of the above. 

Usinn the lavaan() function, yes, but starting measEq.syntax() will free the factor variance at Time 2 when long.equal= includes "loadings".  That is the purpose of this syntax-writer.
My understanding was there are two "levels" of strict invariance, one being factor variances and the other being item residuals

Perhaps you are thinking of establishing equal scale reliability across occasions.  Equal reliability implies strict invariance (equality of residual variances) and homogeneity of factor variances.  But measurement invariance (metric, scalar, strict) is only about the measurement parameters (loadings, intercepts, and residual variances).
I tried all three ID.fac methods and none of them change the results

Indeed, they are all statistically equivalent, so the LRT comparing nested models should not depend on the arbitrary identification method.  Different identification methods do yield different SEs and tests for individual parameters, so when full invariance is rejected, follow-up tests of individual indicators will depend on the identification method, as well as the test statistic (score, Wald, or LRT).  I usually recommend the fixed-factor approach, because the marker-variable method assumes the marker variable is invariant, and the effects-coding approach assumes the "average loading" is equivalent across occasions.  But even fixed-factor is problematic if you test each indicator assuming all others are invariant (i.e., by freeing one indicator at a time).  To get around that, you can first empirically identify a couple of "anchor" indicators, as described in Woods (2009) in the context of IRT:

Woods, C. M. (2009). Empirical selection of anchors for tests of differential item functioning. Applied Psychological Measurement, 33(1), 42-57.

The procedure generalizes to CFA, as well as to RFA/MIMIC-model approaches to testing invariance (e.g.: https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13428-018-1151-3 )

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
